item.title: CRTC says Bell, Telus and Rogers violated its ban on junk fees
item.description: Canada’s telecommunications regulator has determined the Big Three providers violated its rules banning so-called junk fees and is ordering the companies to remove those charges by Dec. 27.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: Canada’s telecommunications regulator has determined the Big Three providers violated its rules banning so-called junk fees and is ordering the companies to remove those charges by Dec. 27. The CRTC issued a ruling Friday saying that carriers violated its prohibition on charging a fee for providing and setting up cellphones when signing up for a service plan. The regulator previously said the companies could face monetary penalties of up to $10 million while relevant managers could be penalized up to $25,000. The CRTC launched a review in June, requiring Bell Canada, Telus Corp. and Rogers Communications Inc. to demonstrate their fees do not contravene its policy. The new regulations came into effect June 12 prohibiting activation, modification and cancellation fees in a bid to make it easier for customers to switch internet and cellphone plans without having to worry about unexpected costs. At the time, the CRTC warned each of the companies over their recently introduced fees, saying the charges did not appear to qualify for an exemption to the new policy meant for optional services or equipment customers choose to purchase. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 27, 2026. Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press BNN Bloomberg, CTV News and CP24 are owned by Bell Media, which is a division of BCE.

item.title: Corus Entertainment reports $59.4M Q4 loss, revenue also lower
item.description: Corus Entertainment Inc. reported a net loss attributable to shareholders of $59.4 million in its latest quarter as the company behind Global Television saw its revenue fall 11 per cent compared with ...
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: TORONTO — Corus Entertainment Inc. reported a net loss attributable to shareholders of $59.4 million in its latest quarter as the company behind Global Television saw its revenue fall 11 per cent compared with a year ago. The television and radio broadcaster says the loss amounted to 30 cents per diluted share for the quarter ended Aug. 31. The result compared with a loss of $277 million or $1.39 per diluted share for the same quarter last year. Chief executive John Gossling says the results reflected significant improvement in advertising revenue trends and the best quarterly performance year-over-year since the second quarter of fiscal 2023. On an adjusted basis, Corus says it lost 20 cents per share in its latest quarter compared with an adjusted loss of 36 cents per share a year earlier. Revenue for what was the company’s fourth quarter totalled $206.8 million, down from $232 million a year earlier. The company says it will receive $36 million as part of Ottawa’s funding support of Canadian local news sectors announced during the federal budget. Corus says the amount will be reflected in its fiscal first quarter of 2027. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 27, 2026.

item.title: Black Friday arrives as budgets tighten, shoppers expected to spend less
item.description: Over the course of the Black Friday weekend, Shopify is expecting Canadians to spend an average $259, down from $282 last year. By the time the holiday season winds down, the retail council projects ...
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: Shoppers are expected to flood malls and websites today as Black Friday gets underway. The annual shopping frenzy delivers promotions and discounts to consumers but arrives this year as the tariff war and conflict in Iran are driving up prices and straining budgets. Over the course of the Black Friday weekend, Shopify is expecting Canadians to spend an average $259, down from $282 last year. By the time the holiday season winds down, the retail council projects Canadians will have spent an average of $911, down from $975 last year. The council’s summer online survey of 2,500 shoppers suggests purchases made during Black Friday and the subsequent Cyber Monday will each make up 29 per cent of holiday budgets. Both Shopify and the council predict value will be a top priority for shoppers this year. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 27, 2026. Tara Deschamps, The Canadian Press

item.title: Auto sector in Canada is moving away from U.S. imports: DesRosiers
item.description: A new report suggests the Canadian auto sector is starting to pivot away from U.S. imports toward other global markets amid the ongoing trade war.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: A new report suggests the Canadian auto sector is starting to pivot away from U.S. imports toward other global markets amid the ongoing trade war. The data analysis from DesRosiers Automotive Consultants showed that light vehicle imports from the United States have accounted for 40 per cent of Canada’s total thus far in 2026 when measured by dollars. That result is down from 49.1 per cent of Canada’s light vehicle imports in 2024. Meanwhile, most other markets saw their shares rise from two years ago. The proportion of Canada’s light vehicle imports from Mexico increased from 16.7 per cent in 2024 to 20.5 per cent so far this year, while Japan saw an increase to 12.9 per cent from 10.7 per cent in 2024. Imports from South Korea have risen from 10.4 to 12.5 per cent, and the combined European markets saw a bump from 9.8 to 11.1 per cent. Aside from Canada’s southern neighbour, China was the only market behind its 2024 share at 2.6 per cent thus far in 2026, down from 2.9 per cent. The overall shift is notable given that not all manufacturers are affected by Canada’s counter-tariffs, which exclude some of the highest volume players, the report said. DesRosiers managing partner Andrew King said certain manufacturers affected by the tariff situation “have moved rapidly to seek other sourcing where possible and to continue to provide Canadians with vehicles at the best possible price.” “What the U.S. lost in share was captured readily by the other major light vehicle exporters, with the trade war helping to diversify Canada’s sourcing in this space,” he said in a statement. Vehicles made in Canada are tariffed by the United States at 25 per cent, minus their American content, while auto and truck parts that comply with the Canada-United States-Mexico agreement on trade are exempt.  In August, President Donald Trump threatened to hike tariffs on all vehicles, auto parts and steel from Canada to 50 per cent on Jan. 1. Canada maintains import duties of 25 per cent on U.S. autos that are not compliant with CUSMA. Ottawa allows automakers to import a quota of vehicles made in the United States tariff-free, based in part on their level of automotive assembly in Canada. Automotive analyst Daniel Ross said the figures show manufacturers are “fighting ... to keep prices from climbing.” “I think it’s directly related to trade policy and the trade war at hand,” said Ross, senior manager of auto industry insights at Canadian Black Book. “A lot of manufacturers are finding their way to decrease dependency for the Canadian market based off of what’s happening in the U.S. So the narrative is, ultimately, where else can we get these? Where is it easier? Where can we work with?” Prime Minister Mark Carney said in recent weeks that trade talks with the U.S. are making progress, but Ottawa won’t accept a deal that doesn’t allow for a viable auto sector. That came three months after Canada pulled out of trade talks with the U.S. due to last-minute demands from Washington that included a hit to Canada’s auto sector. Whether automakers continue to shift imports to non-U.S. markets will depend on how trade negotiations progress, said Ross. “If it were not to move (in a positive) direction, then I think we could continue to see that climb of market share for Mexico, for Japan specifically,” he said. “Whether or not that’s the best way forward, it’s a better way forward than having our skin in the game with a U.S. marketplace that’s highly volatile for the last few years.” --- Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 25, 2026.
